title: Sudan: Devastating RSF drone strikes on civilians in El Obeid should be investigated as war crimes
content:
Drone strikes by Rapid Support Forces (RSF), which hit residential areas and civilian infrastructure in El Obeid city, in Sudan’s North Kordofan State, killing dozens and disrupting essential services, should be investigated as war crimes, Amnesty International said today.

The organization investigated nine RSF drone strikes in El Obeid and its surroundings, which killed 37 civilians and injured 10 between June and August 2026. Three of the strikes hit residential areas; four struck key civilian infrastructure, including El Obeid’s power plant, fuel stations, and the main market; and two targeted moving vehicles. In all incidents, interviewees said they either saw or heard the drones, moments before or after the strikes. Amnesty International’s investigation did not identify military objectives in the vicinity of the sites at the time they were struck.

title: Italy: “A bleak day for freedom of expression” as parliament votes through repressive definition of antisemitism into law
content:
Reacting to a vote by Italy’s parliament to formally adopt the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA) working definition of antisemitism, Erika Guevara Rosas, Amnesty International’s Senior Director for Research, Policy, Advocacy and Campaigns, said: 

“Today marks a bleak day for freedom of expression as Italy explicitly makes the IHRA working definition of antisemitism legally binding. The new law, based on a definition that has long raised serious concerns because it conflates antisemitism with legitimate criticism of Israel, heightens the risk of far-reaching forms of censorship and self-censorship. Its application across schools, universities, social media platforms and beyond threatens a chilling effect and infringe on the rights to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly.

title: Türkiye: LGBTI rights defenders must be immediately released and charges against them dropped
content:
Ahead of the start of a hearing tomorrow in the case against the founders of the LGBTI organization Social Policy, Gender Identity and Sexual Orientation Studies Association (SPoD), the Human Rights Defenders Solidarity Network – a network of 38 organizations including Amnesty International Türkiye – have issued a joint statement. Esther Major, Amnesty International’s Deputy Regional Director for Europe, said: 

“It is deeply disturbing that four founding members of this organization, which has fought tirelessly against discrimination on the grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity, are facing prison sentences for doing this vital work. These could be the first of many such prosecutions in the wake of a new LGBTI crackdown that threatens the existence of dozens of other organizations.

title: El Salvador: Public debt is mortgaging the country’s future without guaranteeing rights today
content:
The increase in public debt and indebtedness in El Salvador over the last decade has not led to a proportional and sustainable improvement in access to economic and social rights, according to Amnesty International’s new report, “When the budget does not guarantee rights”. 

The report analyses the evolution of the public budget between 2015 and 2025, documenting how the increasing debt burden, lack of transparency and a concentration of decision-making power within the executive branch have reduced the state’s capacity to mobilize the maximum of its available resources to uphold rights such as the right to health, to education and to social protection. 

“The findings highlight an alarming contradiction: the Salvadoran state is spending more and increasing its indebtedness, but these available resources do not manifest as equivalent improvements for the population. When debt servicing accounts for a larger proportion of the budget than health or education, it is legitimate to question where the money is going and why,” said Ana Piquer, Americas director at Amnesty International.

title: Azerbaijan: Abzas Media staff endure three years behind bars for independent journalism
content:
Ahead of the third anniversary of the earliest arrests of Abzas Media journalists in Azerbaijan, Marie Struthers, Amnesty International’s Eastern Europe and Central Asia Director, said:

“Three years on, seven Abzas Media journalists remain behind bars in desperate conditions, far from their families. They were among the first targets in what has become a sweeping crackdown on independent journalism in Azerbaijan.

“The reprisals do not end with unfounded imprisonment. Relatives and lawyers report increased use of solitary confinement, denial of health care, beatings and other ill-treatment against the Abzas Media journalists and others jailed for critical journalism and dissenting views.

“The Azerbaijani authorities must immediately and unconditionally release all those imprisoned solely for the exercise of their right to freedom of expression. They must provide all prisoners with adequate health care, promptly investigate reports of abuse and put an end to all forms of ill-treatment.”

title: Saudi Arabia/UN: Closure of ILO complaint a blow for migrant workers facing persistent abuse and discrimination
content:
Responding to the closure of the labour rights complaint filed against Saudi Arabia under Article 26 of the International Labour Organization (ILO) Constitution, following an agreement reached between Saudi Arabia and workers’ representative to the ILO, Iain Byrne, Amnesty International’s Head of Economic and Social Justice, said: 

“The premature closure of the formal complaint at the ILO against Saudi Arabia is a blow for the millions of migrant workers in the country.  

“The concerns that gave rise to the complaint remain unresolved. They include serious abuses linked to the persistence of the kafala system, which continues to leave migrant workers dependent on their employers and enables forced labour, exploitation and racial discrimination, while imposing substantial barriers to accessing justice.  

“While the agreement reached between the trade unions and the government sets out broad areas for future engagement, it fails to detail any specific legal or policy changes that Saudi Arabia has committed to undertake. It also fails so far to provide clear timelines for action, publicly available benchmarks or an independent monitoring mechanism.

title: Europe: Disgraceful Rwanda deportation deal repeats mistakes of the past
content:
Reacting to today’s announcement from the Vienna Migration Conference where Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands announced plans to carry out deportations to so-called “return hubs” in Rwanda, Aimée Stuflesser, the asylum and migration expert at Amnesty International Austria, said:

“Today’s disgraceful deportation deal between European countries and Rwanda repeats mistakes of the past. Sending people to a country they have never been to is irresponsible and there is a real danger that the Rwanda deal will, with its limited chance for scrutiny, become a cruel black hole for human rights.

“Undocumented people must not become pawns in a politics of deterrence. The harms of these types of migration deals are well documented. From the Italy–Albania deal and the UK’s attempt to forcibly send people to Rwanda, to Australia’s offshore detention system, past attempts to send people to countries to which they have no connection have proven unlawful, unworkable and expensive.

title: Can EU Action Against TikTok Rabbit Holes Lead to Real Social Media Design Change?
content:
The European Union’s executive preliminarily found TikTok in breach of the Digital Services Act (DSA) for failing to adequately assess and mitigate the risk of users falling into rabbit holes that could harm their well-being. The Commission particularly raised concern about young users’ and vulnerable adults’ repeated exposure to content that can negatively affect people’s mental health. 

The TikTok case is the latest investigation by the EU under the Digital Services Act, focusing on the platform’s alleged issues with harmful rabbit holes created by design in its highly personalized ‘For You’ feed. It signals that regulators are finally demanding fundamental changes to the inherently toxic design shared by many of the leading social media platforms. It is time to stop tinkering around the edges and set out clear rules for a safer, rights-respecting tech landscape.

title: Saudi Arabia: Amazon warehouse workers still facing exploitation despite company initiatives
content:
Migrant workers hired to work in Amazon’s operations in Saudi Arabia continue to face abuses from the third-party labour supply companies that employ them. They are also subjected to harsh working conditions in Amazon’s warehouses and the risk of the company ending their assignment at will, despite Amazon’s attempts to improve other aspects of their recruitment and living conditions, Amnesty International said in a new briefing today.

Amazon in Saudi Arabia: Why migrant workers remain at risk of exploitation documented some important improvements, including reduced recruitment-fee abuses, better accommodation standards and improved access to grievance mechanisms. Following Amnesty International’s 2023 investigation, Amazon also reimbursed more than USD 2.45 million to 1,180 workers in Saudi Arabia. Nevertheless, migrant workers remain vulnerable to exploitation under Amazon’s hiring model.

title: What’s the difference between being not racist and being anti-racist?
content:
There is a big difference between being not racist and anti-racist.

Perhaps you can recall a time when you heard someone saying something racist, or acting racist. Non-racist people don’t want to rock the boat. They wouldn’t confront the antagonizer. Rather than saying what they think, they would stay silent and maybe talk about what happened after.

Anti-racists look around and think about what they can do, what tools they have, or what they can say to make it clear that racist behaviour is unacceptable. That doesn’t mean they are rude to people but that they will call people out in a polite way when they hear racist language or see racist behaviour.

Being anti-racist also means looking beyond individual behaviour. Anti-racists look at the roots of systemic racism in power, policies, institutions and histories, and see how they can produce or sustain racial hierarchies and inequalities.

This means that being not racist is about what you don’t do and being anti-racist is about how do you understand, acknowledge, challenge and take action to change unequal systems that produce racial inequality.

title: Russia: Lev Shlosberg’s outrageous 11-year prison sentence for anti-war views upheld
content:
Reacting to a court’s decision to uphold the guilty verdict and 11 years and one month prison sentence of Lev Shlosberg, a leading member of the Yabloko party – the only party in Russia to stand on an anti-war platform – for sharing social media posts related to Russia’s war on Ukraine, Marie Struthers, Amnesty International’s Director for Eastern Europe and Central Asia, said:

“According to this verdict, someone who expresses pacifist views and shares a photo of a victim of Putin’s aggression against Ukraine is guilty of ‘discrediting the Armed Forces’ and ‘spreading false information.’ This tells you all you need to know about the state of freedom of expression in today’s Russia.

“Today’s decision follows the persecution of other Yabloko members, and the disqualification of the party from the recent State Duma election. Expressing any anti-war sentiment is becoming increasingly dangerous in Russia.”

“Amnesty International calls for the immediate and unconditional release of Lev Shlosberg and all those detained solely for exercising their right to freedom of expression and demands an end to the systemic repression of peaceful political dissent.”

title: Angola: Authorities must immediately release General Nila and four other members of UNTRA
content:
Reacting to the 11 November arrest of Serrote José de Oliveira, also known as General Nila, Angolan activist and leader of the National Unity for the Total Revolution of Angola (UNTRA) movement, and four other movement members during a ceremony to commemorate six years since the fatal shooting of Inocêncio de Matos by security forces during a protest, Amnesty International’s Regional Director for East and Southern Africa, Tigere Chagutah, said:

“The arrest of General Nila and four other members of UNTRA while they were peacefully participating in a ceremony is a contravention of the right to freedom of peaceful assembly.

title: “The thrill of being organized and acting together will overcome hopelessness”: Meet Deniz Gümüşel and hear about the struggle to protect the Akbelen Forest, Türkiye
content:
For more than a decade, Deniz Gümüşel, an environmental engineer by profession, has worked with civil society organizations documenting the environmental, health and human rights impacts of fossil fuels across Türkiye. In the last seven years, Deniz has joined local communities opposing the coal mining operations in Muğla province in south-western Türkiye, a region that hosts dozens of coal mines and three coal-fired power stations. Their struggle is intertwined with the protection of the Akbelen Forest, as a symbol of resistance against the expansion of coal mining in the region.

Like many other environmental human rights defenders (EHRDs), Deniz’s activism has come at a personal cost. Over the years, she has been subject to multiple criminal investigations and prosecutions for her peaceful environmental activism in defence of İkizköy and Akbelen Forest.

The İkizköy community’s struggle, of which Deniz was a part, delayed the cutting down of Akbelen Forest for four years, until it was destroyed in 2023.  Yet they continue to resist, to protect the village’s farmland and olive groves.
